title: Supreme Court Term Limits
hook: U.S. Supreme Court justices serve for life — unusual among democracies. A recurring reform would swap that for fixed terms. Why the idea keeps returning, and why it's so hard to enact.
key_points: Article III of the U.S. Constitution gives federal judges tenure 'during good Behaviour' — in practice, life tenure ending only in death, retirement, or impeachment.
That makes the U.S. unusual: most peer democracies cap top-court service with fixed terms or a mandatory retirement age.
Life tenure means vacancies open unpredictably, so how many justices a president appoints is partly a matter of timing and luck.
The most-discussed reform is 18-year staggered terms — one seat opening every two years, giving each president two appointments per term.
Because life tenure is written into the Constitution, most scholars think term limits would need a constitutional amendment — a very high bar.
In 2026, congressional Democrats renewed a push for term limits; the debate pits regular turnover against protecting judicial independence.
content_html: Supreme Court justices, like all U.S. federal judges, hold their seats for life. The Constitution says they serve "during good Behaviour," which in practice means until they die, retire, or are impeached — and impeachment has never removed a justice. That single design choice drives a reform debate that resurfaces every few years.
extra_html: The consequence of life tenure is that vacancies open up unpredictably — whenever a justice dies or chooses to step down — so the number of justices a president gets to appoint is partly a matter of timing and luck. Reformers argue this makes each appointment enormously high-stakes and turns confirmation into a bitter fight. The most commonly floated fix is a system of 18-year staggered terms: with nine justices, one term would end every two years, giving each president exactly two appointments per four-year term and making turnover regular rather than random. The U.S. is an outlier here — most other constitutional democracies limit top-court service with fixed terms or a mandatory retirement age. The catch is that life tenure is embedded in Article III of the Constitution, so most legal scholars think imposing term limits would require a constitutional amendment, which needs supermajorities in Congress and ratification by three-quarters of the states. In 2026, per SCOTUSblog, congressional Democrats renewed a push for term limits; the underlying arguments are perennial — supporters say fixed terms would lower the stakes and depoliticize the Court, while critics warn that restructuring the Court could threaten the judicial independence life tenure is meant to protect. (This card describes the U.S. federal judiciary specifically.)

flashcards.prompt: Why does the Constitution's 'good Behaviour' clause effectively give Supreme Court justices life tenure?
flashcards.back_html: Article III lets federal judges keep their seats "during good Behaviour" — so they serve until death, retirement, or impeachment, and no justice has ever been removed by impeachment.

flashcards.prompt: What is the most commonly proposed reform to Supreme Court life tenure?

choices.text: 18-year staggered terms, giving each president two appointments per term
Letting the president fire justices at will
Electing justices by nationwide popular vote

flashcards.explanation_html: Staggered 18-year terms would open one seat every two years, turning random vacancies into a regular, predictable schedule.

flashcards.prompt: Why do most scholars think Supreme Court term limits would be hard to enact?

choices.text: Life tenure is written into the Constitution, so changing it likely needs a constitutional amendment
A simple majority vote in one chamber of Congress could do it immediately
It would only require the sitting justices' consent

flashcards.explanation_html: Because Article III grants life tenure, imposing term limits likely requires a constitutional amendment — supermajorities in Congress plus ratification by three-quarters of the states.
